summary: Recovered a material finding from the blocked 2026-10-07T15:13:32Z Macro run. The New York Fed September Survey of Consumer Expectations raised median one-year inflation expectations to 3.9% from 3.6%, the highest since May 2023; three-year expectations rose to 3.3% from 3.2%, while five-year expectations remained 3.0%. This supports REACCELERATING_NEAR_TERM_WITH_LONG_RUN_ANCHOR_INTACT, not full de-anchoring. Long-duration Treasury yields simultaneously remained near 24-year highs, increasing the relevance of the expectation shift for discount-rate assumptions.
net_new_delta: A verified consumer-inflation-expectations state change: near-term expectations reaccelerated materially while the five-year anchor held.

evidence.source: Federal Reserve Bank of New York
evidence.finding: Median inflation expectations increased 0.3 percentage point to 3.9% at one year and 0.1 point to 3.3% at three years; five-year expectations were unchanged at 3.0%. The one-year reading is the highest since May 2023.

evidence.source: Reuters reporting the New York Fed survey
evidence.finding: Households expected higher price gains across gas, food, rent, medical care, and college costs and downgraded current and future finances; labor-market expectations were more constructive.
The U.S. 30-year Treasury yield touched 5.7041%, a 24-year high, with global yields pressured by inflation and fiscal concerns.
Crude inventories fell 3.2 million barrels, gasoline rose 0.4 million, and distillates were little changed; mixed products and muted price response did not establish a separate oil-inventory regime.

Update research context to REACCELERATING_NEAR_TERM_WITH_LONG_RUN_ANCHOR_INTACT. The one-year rise matters for nominal-rate and equity-duration assumptions, but the unchanged five-year reading does not support full expectation de-anchoring.

conflicts: Five-year expectations remained at 3.0%, contradicting a claim of broad long-run de-anchoring.
The Treasury selloff predates the survey release and also reflects fiscal, oil, issuance, and term-premium concerns; causality cannot be assigned to the survey alone.
Mixed EIA product inventories and muted incremental oil response do not establish a separate inventory shock.
unknowns: Persistence of the one-year expectation increase
